                  Human

                  Tier 0 · 3 Edges · None

                  Adaptable, socially restless, and remarkably willing to challenge established institutions. Three centuries of corridor travel have scattered humanity across dozens of colonies, governments and movements: generous and ruthless, often in the same crew.

                  Suggested skills: Commerce, Diplomacy, Piloting, Firearms.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Venture Spirit +2 to Commerce to fund, pitch or rescue a risky enterprise. Overreach. You bet bigger than you should. Accept the loss when the gamble turns.
                  Restless +2 to Survival or Navigation when going where older peoples won’t. Impatient with Tradition. Old customs bore you. Accept the offense you cause.
                  Second Chances +2 to Diplomacy to talk someone out of a ruinous debt, grudge or deal. Soft Touch. You can’t refuse someone in need. Accept the cost of helping.

                  Vesh

                  Tier 0 · 3 Edges · Body −1, Agility +1

                  Slender quadrupeds who handle tools with prehensile sensory tendrils, and who reached the corridors only 24 years ago. Their governments struggle to stay independent while learning from civilizations thousands of years older, and humans recognize the struggle.

                  Species rules:

                  • Quick on four legs: Move +1.

                  Suggested skills: Diplomacy, Science, Athletics, Sensors.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Fresh Eyes +2 to Investigation to notice what old hands take for granted. Newcomer. You don’t know the rules everyone else knows. Accept the gaffe.
                  Sensory Tendrils +2 to Sensors to feel air currents and nearby movement. Homeworld Politics. Your government wants a favor. Accept the request.
                  Fleet-Footed +2 to Athletics to run or leap. Easily Exploited. Everyone has a deal for you. Accept the bad bargain.

                  Brulvek

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body +1, Agility −1, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Low, broad hexapods with powerful manipulator limbs and thick insulating hides, evolved among volcanoes and corrosive air. They built the Hegemony’s shipyards; their engineers are sought everywhere for restoring machines centuries past replacement parts.

                  Species rules:

                  • Furnace hide: heat, smoke and corrosive air mark one fewer box and don’t impair you.

                  Suggested skills: Engineering, Science, Athletics, Commerce.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Old Machines +2 to Engineering to repair or restore ancient or unfamiliar machinery. Syndicate Ties. Your syndicate calls in a favor. Accept the job.
                  Forge-Born +2 to Survival in heat, fire and toxic environments. Imperial Contract. Someone still pays your people to serve the empire. Accept the conflict.
                  Six Strong Limbs +2 to Athletics to lift, haul or brace. Dying Industry. Home is failing. Accept the plea for money or help.

                  Corvani

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Agility −1, Intellect +1, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Radially arranged, five-limbed beings with photosensitive skin, from forests where cooperation meant survival. They treat technology as ecology, and their restoration teams heal worlds the Hegemony stripped, often against mining corporations.

                  Species rules:

                  • Photosynthetic: after days without light you weaken (−1 to all rolls) until you rest under light.

                  Suggested skills: Science, Medicine, Survival, Engineering.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Restorer +2 to Science to heal or understand a damaged ecosystem. Ecological Safeguards. You won’t let a world be poisoned. Accept the fight.
                  Living Tech +2 to Engineering with biological or grown technology. Sunstarved. Dark ships and stations drain you. Accept the weakness.
                  Symbiosis +2 to Medicine with biotech and alien biology. Corporate Enemies. Mining companies know your face. Accept their lawyers or worse.

                  Draelin

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility +1, Intellect +1, Will −1

                  Long, serpentine beings with two long arms and no legs, who sense electromagnetic fields, from a world of wild magnetic fields. Their cartographic guilds keep the best corridor charts in known space, and have sold them to both sides of more than one war.

                  Species rules:

                  • Field sense: feel electromagnetic fields, live wiring and active machinery nearby.
                  • Navigation is Trained for free.

                  Free skill: Navigation is always at least Trained and doesn’t use a Trained pick.

                  Suggested skills: Navigation, Sensors, Commerce, Piloting.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Guild Charts +2 to Navigation on charted corridors. Sold Out. Your guild sells your secrets to the other side. Accept the betrayal.
                  Field Reader +2 to Sensors to find hidden machinery or follow a power line. Public or Private?. You must decide who gets safe passage. Accept the guild’s anger.
                  Serpentine +2 to Athletics to squeeze, coil and climb where legs can’t. Magnetic Storms. Strong fields disorient you. Accept the stumble.

                  Joruun

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body +1, Agility −1, Intellect −1, Will +1

                  Tall, powerful bipeds with thick skin, sensory ridges and acute hearing, from a cold, storm-wracked world. Their confederation has fought the Hegemony for centuries, built to keep resisting after its leaders fall.

                  Species rules:

                  • Cold-hardy: cold and storms don’t impair you.

                  Suggested skills: Firearms, Leadership, Survival, Sensors.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Keen Hearing +2 to Sensors by sound. The Confederation Calls. Your league needs you. Accept the call to arms.
                  Fight On +2 to Leadership to rally others after a leader falls. Old Grudge. You hate the Hegemony. Accept the reckless choice.
                  Junction Defender +2 to Firearms when holding a fortified position. Blunt. You say what you think. Accept the offense.

                  Kel

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Intellect +1, Presence −2, Will +1

                  Chitin-plated social beings raised in immense hive-cities, analytical and cooperative. The Kel homeworld is burdened by inherited Tessan debt; their search for new markets triggered humanity’s First Contact Crisis. Kel society is split between loyalists, reformers and radicals.

                  Species rules:

                  • Hive-raised: after a day alone, −1 to all rolls until back among others.
                  • Hard to read: others take −2 to Psychology to read a Kel’s mood.

                  Suggested skills: Science, Commerce, Navigation, Computers.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Hive Analysis +2 to Investigation or Science when working with at least one ally. Isolation Dread. Being cut off from others unnerves you. Accept the panic or the poor choice.
                  Chemical Signals +2 to Psychology to read another Kel, or to coordinate a group by scent and posture. Every Gift a Contract. You expect every favor repaid. Accept the misunderstanding it causes.
                  Debt-Born +2 to Commerce to find who owes whom. The Homeworld’s Debt. Your world’s creditors, or its radicals, want your help. Accept the call.

                  Mirrun

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility +1

                  Smooth-skinned amphibians from a deep-ocean world, agile swimmers famous for their humor. Their skin detects minute pressure changes; Mirrun researchers lead the field in gravimetric resonance detection.

                  Species rules:

                  • Amphibious: breathe water and swim at running speed; your skin must stay moist (−1 to all rolls after a day dry).

                  Suggested skills: Sensors, Science, Athletics, Diplomacy.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Pressure Sense +2 to Sensors to feel movement, engines or corridor resonance through a hull or floor. Ocean Guardian. You can’t stand by while a sea is poisoned. Accept the fight with the extractors.
                  Deep Swimmer +2 to Athletics in water and zero-g. Dry Air. Arid worlds wear you down. Accept the misery.
                  Disarming Laugh +2 to Diplomacy to defuse a tense meeting with a joke. Can’t Stay Serious. The joke comes out at the wrong moment. Accept the offense.

                  Ommek

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −2, Agility +1, Intellect +1

                  Small, heavily articulated beings with many fine manipulators and exquisite touch, makers of robots, AI and automated ships. Their technocratic republics demand review of every major technology, and their defenses have made conquest too expensive.

                  Species rules:

                  • Fine manipulators: Engineering is Trained for free.

                  Free skill: Engineering is always at least Trained and doesn’t use a Trained pick.

                  Suggested skills: Engineering, Computers, Sensors, Science.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Exquisite Touch +2 to Engineering for precision work. Review Required. You insist on checking first. Accept the delay.
                  Robot Maker +2 to Computers with robots, drones and AI. Imperial Interest. The Hegemony wants your knowledge. Accept the spy or the kidnapper.
                  Layered Defenses +2 to Engineering or Computers to secure a position or system. Small Frame. You’re easily overpowered. Accept the danger.

                  Shivar

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −2, Intellect +1, Will +1

                  Tall, narrow beings of translucent tissue whose nervous systems share emotions in synchronized pulses. Their theology reads the corridors as cosmic order; their schism, between imperial zealots and moderates who see a universe of change, has fueled wars inside the Hegemony.

                  Species rules:

                  • Empath: you share emotions instantly with nearby Shivar, and feel the strong emotions of anyone close by. (Empathy, not psionics.)

                  Suggested skills: Psychology, Diplomacy, Science, Leadership.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Deep Empathy +2 to Psychology to read anyone’s feelings nearby. Flooded. Strong emotions around you overwhelm you. Accept the distraction.
                  Corridor Theology +2 to Science or Navigation to read meaning in corridor patterns. Schism. Zealots or moderates want you on their side. Accept the pressure.
                  Pulse of Calm +2 to Diplomacy to calm a frightened or angry crowd. Translucent. Your feelings show through your skin. Accept the lie that fails.

                  Tessan

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body +1, Agility −2, Will +1

                  Large, scaled, exceptionally long-lived beings for whom contractual obligation is the foundation of civilization. Tessan dynasties lend, insure and arbitrate across hundreds of worlds; contact with humanity has split them between traditional creditors and reformers.

                  Species rules:

                  • Long-lived: a Tessan remembers deals made before most humans’ grandparents were born.
                  • Bond: a contract a Tessan swears to is binding in law throughout Tessan space.

                  Suggested skills: Commerce, Diplomacy, Psychology, Leadership.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Ledger Memory +2 to Commerce to recall a debt, contract or precedent. Bound by Contract. Your word binds you even when it hurts. Accept the cost of keeping it.
                  Old Scales Once per scene, a hit that would mark 1 box marks none. Slow to Move. Your bulk and age make haste hard. Accept being left behind or late.
                  Dynasty Name +2 to Diplomacy with those who owe your family. Family Debts. Your dynasty’s obligations become yours. Accept the duty when it calls.

                  Thrum

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility −1, Presence +1, Will +1

                  Broad, soft-bodied beings whose internal cavities make low-frequency resonance; they speak in overlapping harmonies humans can’t reproduce. Their acoustic science found the patterns in corridor fluctuations; they refuse to let it become weapons.

                  Species rules:

                  • Resonance: speak and hear through walls and floors; you need a translator for most other languages.

                  Suggested skills: Sensors, Science, Diplomacy, Navigation.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Echo Sense +2 to Sensors to map a space or find a void by sound. Pacifist Science. You won’t let your work become a weapon. Accept the cost of refusing.
                  Chorus Voice +2 to Leadership or Diplomacy addressing a group. Lost in Translation. Translators mangle you. Accept the misunderstanding.
                  Pattern Listener +2 to Navigation or Science reading corridor fluctuations. Soft Body. You bruise easily. Accept the injury.

                  Uth

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body +1, Agility −1, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Compact, thick-skinned beings with broad manipulators and complex chemical senses, whose civilization the Hegemony destroyed millennia ago. Uth communities live everywhere, keeping family history and memory; many work to reclaim their worlds, many refuse to be defined by loss.

                  Species rules:

                  • Chemical senses: identify people and substances by scent.

                  Suggested skills: Investigation, Streetwise, Medicine, Diplomacy.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Scent Tracker +2 to Investigation to track or identify by scent. Ancestral Worlds. The reclamation movement asks your help. Accept the call.
                  Diaspora Network +2 to Streetwise to find an Uth community and its help in any port. Old Wound. The Hegemony’s name sets you off. Accept the reckless choice.
                  Family Memory +2 to Diplomacy using shared history or old obligations. Defined by Loss. Others see only your people’s history. Accept the frustration.

                  Uxarra

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Agility +1, Presence −1

                  Flexible, partly hydrostatic beings whose skin changes color, texture and sheen. Their homeworld’s wild climates made them adaptable and self-reliant, and their camouflage has earned them an unfair reputation for deceit.

                  Species rules:

                  • Chromatic skin: change color and texture at will.

                  Suggested skills: Stealth, Survival, Athletics, Medicine.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Camouflage +2 to Stealth when still or moving slowly. Distrusted. Others assume you’re hiding something. Accept the suspicion.
                  Adaptable Body +2 to Survival in extreme or changing environments. Restless Home. You can’t settle. Accept the urge to move on.
                  Rescue Specialist +2 to Athletics or Medicine to reach and save someone in a disaster. Won’t Leave Anyone. You go back for the last one. Accept the risk.

                  Vael

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −2, Agility +1, Intellect +1

                  Long, light-boned beings with four manipulator limbs, born in low gravity. Their homeworld died in an ancient stellar catastrophe; their living fleets now roam the corridors trading, repairing and carrying peoples between systems.

                  Species rules:

                  • Zero-g native: no penalty in zero gravity.
                  • Low-gravity body: −1 to physical rolls in standard gravity without an exo-frame.

                  Suggested skills: Piloting, Engineering, Commerce, Navigation.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Void Dancer +2 to Athletics and Firearms in zero-g. Fleet First. The flotilla’s needs come before yours. Accept the call.
                  Fleet Trader +2 to Commerce in flotilla markets and ports. Planetbound Misery. Gravity wells exhaust you. Accept the strain.
                  Generation Ship Wisdom +2 to Engineering to keep a habitat or ship running on nothing. Suspect Neutrality. Every side doubts the fleets. Accept the search or the suspicion.

                  Veyari

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility −1, Intellect +2

                  Small bipedal scholars with long, delicate fingers, soft scales and brains built for associative memory. Their neutral archives hold lost corridor data and ancient claims, which is why empires, corporations and zealots keep trying to seize them.

                  Species rules:

                  • Associative memory: recall anything you have experienced in detail.

                  Suggested skills: Investigation, Science, Computers, Diplomacy.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Living Archive +2 to Science or Investigation to recall history, precedent or old data. Knowledge Must Survive. You won’t let records be destroyed. Accept the risk to save them.
                  Archivist’s Neutrality +2 to Diplomacy to be accepted as neutral by both sides. Wanted Records. Someone wants what you remember. Accept the pursuit.
                  Perfect Detail +2 to Investigation to spot what changed in a place you’ve seen before. Small and Soft. You’re easy to overpower. Accept the danger.

                  Ylith

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −2, Agility +1, Intellect +1

                  Hollow-boned, feathered gliders with broad wing-membranes and extraordinary vision. Their aerial city-states are renowned for navigation and cartography; confined spaces are profoundly uncomfortable for them.

                  Species rules:

                  • Glide: in normal gravity, glide down any height safely.
                  • Far sight: see detail at many times human range.

                  Suggested skills: Navigation, Sensors, Piloting, Athletics.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Hawk Eye +2 to Sensors and Firearms at long range. Cramped. Tight spaces unsettle you. Accept −2 or the detour.
                  Corridor Spotter +2 to Navigation to find a corridor instruments miss. Sky-Proud. You look down on groundlings. Accept the resentment.
                  Born Flier +2 to Piloting in atmosphere. Fragile Bones. Falls and crushes hurt you more. Accept the injury.

                  Zethri

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility +1

                  Small, agile beings with four limbs, a prehensile tail and broad reflective eyes adapted to dim light. A corridor collapse isolated their colonies for centuries; reconnected, they found strangers who share their name, and now work at reunification.

                  Species rules:

                  • Dim-adapted: see in near-darkness; −1 to Agility-based rolls in bright light.

                  Suggested skills: Engineering, Survival, Stealth, Diplomacy.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Dark Eyes +2 to Sensors and Stealth in darkness. Glare. Bright light blinds you at the worst moment. Accept the stumble.
                  Prehensile Tail +2 to Athletics to climb, hang or hold on in zero-g. Reconnected Strangers. Other Zethri colonies see you as a foreigner. Accept the mistrust.
                  Built to Last +2 to Engineering or Survival to make a place self-sufficient. Many Zethri. Your cluster’s factions disagree about you. Accept the dispute.

                  Zhaq

                  Tier 1 · 2 Edges · Body −1, Agility +1, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Flexible, tripedal beings with segmented limbs and three independently focusing eyes. Isolated for six centuries by a corridor collapse, the Zhaq built free republics, and refused when the Hegemony came back. Their resistance inspires separatists everywhere.

                  Species rules:

                  • Three eyes: watch several directions at once.
                  • Torpor: slow your metabolism to outlast cold, hunger or entombment for weeks.

                  Suggested skills: Sensors, Stealth, Survival, Firearms.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Triple Watch +2 to Sensors to keep watch or spot an ambush. Never Again. You won’t submit to an empire’s demand. Accept the fight.
                  Long Sleep +2 to Survival to endure deprivation in torpor. Separatist Symbol. Your face means rebellion to the Hegemony. Accept the attention.
                  Segmented Limbs +2 to Athletics to squeeze, climb or balance. Six Centuries Behind. Imperial customs you never learned trip you up. Accept the gaffe.

                  Dresh

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Body +2, Agility −1, Intellect −1

                  Dense, four-armed soldiers from a high-gravity world, armored in thick hide. Dresh legions were the Hegemony’s ground forces for millennia; now their protectorates argue whether soldiers owe the throne, their commanders, or the people they protect.

                  Species rules:

                  • Four arms: hold a weapon and still climb, carry or work.
                  • Dermal armor: once per fight, a hit marks one fewer box.
                  • Heavy-world: −1 to physical rolls in low gravity without boots or a frame.

                  Suggested skills: Firearms, Close Combat, Athletics, Leadership.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Legion Drill +2 to Firearms or Close Combat fighting beside an ally. Whose Soldier?. Old loyalties pull at you. Accept the conflict of duty.
                  Four-Armed Grip +2 to Close Combat to grapple or hold. Imperial Habits. Orders come easier than choices. Accept the mistake of obeying.
                  Heavy-World Build +2 to Body rolls to resist injury, fatigue or crushing force. Deserter’s Mark. The Hegemony keeps lists. Accept the bounty hunter.

                  Eshuum

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Body −1, Intellect +1, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Colonial organisms: an Eshuum person is a community of semi-independent biological units joined into one mind. They govern by consensus, and oppose forced separation and experiments on intelligent beings.

                  Species rules:

                  • Detachable units: send a small unit to scout a short distance; it reports what it senses.
                  • Many bodies: once per fight, a hit that would mark 2 or more boxes marks one fewer as units are lost.

                  Suggested skills: Science, Medicine, Diplomacy, Sensors.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Scout Units +2 to Sensors or Stealth using a detached unit. Never Divided. Forced separation is horror to you. Accept the risk to prevent it.
                  Consensus Mind +2 to Psychology to find what a group truly agrees on. Research Target. Hegemony researchers want specimens. Accept the danger.
                  Redistribute +2 to Engineering or Medicine by reshaping units into fine tools. Slow to Decide. You must reach inner consensus. Accept the delay.

                  Khaum

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Body +2, Agility −2, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Massive, eyeless burrowers with sensory whiskers and powerful digging limbs, whose cavern nations run for hundreds of kilometers underground. Cautious and long-planning, they have sheltered refugees from many Hegemony campaigns.

                  Species rules:

                  • Eyeless: perceive by pressure and vibration; darkness means nothing, but you can’t read screens or print without aids.
                  • Burrower: dig through earth and soft rock.
                  • Massive: −2 to Stealth; most doors are too small.

                  Suggested skills: Engineering, Science, Survival, Athletics.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Seismic Sense +2 to Sensors to feel movement, footsteps or tunnels through the ground. Wary of the Open. Open skies and unfamiliar places unsettle you. Accept the hesitation.
                  Deep Digger +2 to Athletics to dig, break or brace rock. Refuge Keeper. You shelter the hunted. Accept the danger they bring.
                  Long Planner +2 to Engineering when you have time to plan. Distrusts Protectors. You refuse protection that demands obedience. Accept the cost.

                  Ozhvek

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Body +2, Agility −2, Presence −1, Will +1

                  Massive, radially symmetrical founders of the Hegemony, on six powerful limbs, with sensory clusters all around their upper bodies and lifespans near five centuries. Their ancient houses are divided over what the empire should become.

                  Species rules:

                  • All-around senses: you can’t be surprised from behind.
                  • Massive: most ships, doors and furniture are too small; −2 to Stealth.

                  Suggested skills: Leadership, Diplomacy, Firearms, Psychology.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Imperial House +2 to Leadership with Hegemony subjects and soldiers. Hated Founders. Every former subject remembers the empire. Accept the hostility.
                  Living Bulwark Once per fight, a hit that would mark 2 or more boxes marks one fewer. Too Big to Hide. You are always noticed. Accept the attention.
                  Hundred Eyes +2 to Sensors and Investigation to notice anything in a room. House Politics. Your house wants something of you. Accept the summons.

                  Qor

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Body +2, Agility −2, Intellect +1, Presence −1

                  Silicon-based beings of slowly growing crystal with distributed nervous systems, speaking by electromagnetic and mechanical oscillation. Masters of materials and computation, the Qor take Tessan capital but refuse debts that threaten sovereignty.

                  Species rules:

                  • Crystalline: immune to vacuum, toxins and disease; you need a translator to speak with most species.
                  • Slow time sense: −1 to Psychology with fast-living peoples.
                  • Heavy crystal: Move −1.

                  Suggested skills: Engineering, Science, Computers, Commerce.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Materials Mastery +2 to Engineering with materials, armor and hull structures. Sovereign. You won’t accept terms that bind your world. Accept the lost deal.
                  Crystal Mind +2 to Computers for long calculations. Alien Time. You misjudge how quickly others act. Accept the delay.
                  Unbreakable +2 to Survival in vacuum and extreme environments. Mineral Wealth. Prospectors eye your homeworld. Accept the confrontation.

                  Sen

                  Tier 2 · 1 Edge · Agility −2, Intellect +1, Presence −1, Will +2

                  Compact, slow-moving beings in layered mineral shells who live more than a thousand years. Their experiments have run for centuries; they have watched empires rise and fall, and their warnings about corridor instability carry great weight.

                  Species rules:

                  • Shell: once per fight, a hit marks one fewer box.
                  • Slow: you always act last in a fight, and Move −1.

                  Suggested skills: Science, Investigation, Navigation, Psychology.

                  Advantage Effect Companion complication
                  Patient Observer +2 to Science or Investigation when you take your time. Out of Step. You think in decades. Accept being too late.
                  Ancient Records +2 to Navigation to predict corridor behavior. Reluctant to Intervene. You’d rather observe than act. Accept the cost of waiting.
                  Unhurried +2 to Will to stay calm under fear, pressure or torture. Shell-Slow. You can’t run. Accept being caught.

                  Making your own

                  The roles and species in this book are a starting point, not a limit. With the GM’s agreement, any player can create their own role or species. The creator has a Custom option at the end of each list, and its checklist holds a custom choice to the same rules as everything else.

                  A custom role

                  A role is a concept, not a package of powers: it gives no bonus of its own. A custom one only needs a clear place in the group.

                  1. Name it and describe it. One sentence for what your character does that no one else does, in the style of the roles above: “Courier: carries what can’t be sent by signal, through corridors no one else will fly.”
                  2. Choose a group. Pick the one it belongs with: Commerce, Frontier, Service, Ship Crew or Trouble. The group only sets your sheet’s colors and emblem.
                  3. Pick four core skills. The skills it can’t do without. Mark them Trained yourself in step 3 (the built-in roles do this for you); they count toward your normal Trained skills.
                  4. Check it with the GM. It should fit the setting and overlap the existing roles as little as possible.

                  In the creator: in step 1, choose Custom role… at the end of the Role list, then enter its name and group. Write the description in What you bring.

                  A custom species

                  Build it with the GM, one step at a time.

                  1. The concept

                  Two or three sentences: where they come from, what sets them apart, and how others see them. It should be something the species in this book don’t already cover.

                  2. The tier

                  The tier measures how much the species gives on its own. Each tier costs one of your 3 Edge points, so stronger species start with fewer Edges.

                  Tier Edges Use it for
                  0 3 Ordinary people: a homeland, upbringing or culture, with no special abilities
                  1 2 One small, constant edge: keen senses, a tough hide, a free Trained skill, resistance to one hazard
                  2 1 Clear inhuman or supernatural gifts: venom, a second form, strong resistances
                  3 0 Remarkable beings: several strong abilities, and serious weaknesses to match

                  When in doubt, choose the higher tier.

                  3. Attribute adjustments

                  Give adjustments from −2 to +2 per attribute that total zero: a +2 needs a −2 or two −1s. The adjustments move the attribute’s base (+1 starts it at 11) and raise its starting maximum (13 plus the bonus). Most species change two to four attributes.

                  A species that is plainly faster or slower on its feet than a human (long-legged, heavy, built for another gravity) may also take a speed adjustment of +1 or −1 to Move. Most have none. It isn’t an attribute adjustment and needn’t balance.

                  4. Core rules (tier 1 and up)

                  One to three short rules that always apply: what they can do (see in the dark, resist cold, a free Trained skill) and what it costs (a weakness, a people’s distrust, a hazard they can’t abide). A strength with no drawback is worth more than it looks, so price it a tier higher.

                  5. Species advantages

                  Write one to three. Each works like a general advantage: +2 to one skill in a narrow situation, or a small, limited permission (“once per scene…”). Each comes with a companion complication: a problem the trait causes, with a clear trigger and a real consequence, which earns a Resolve point when it bites, like any complication. A character takes one advantage, general or species, so make them distinct choices.

                  6. An alternate form (optional, tier 2 or 3)

                  If the species changes shape, give the form attribute bonuses (usually +2 to one attribute and +1 to another), two or three traits, and its drawbacks. A form’s Agility and Body bonuses change its Move, and a fast form may add a speed adjustment of its own. The shared rules for forms in Species apply. The bonuses count only while the character is in that form: the sheet’s form switch shows both sets of numbers.

                  In the creator

                  1. In step 2, choose Custom species… at the end of the Species list.
                  2. Name it, choose the tier you agreed, and set its adjustments. The checklist confirms they total zero.
                  3. Write its core rules in Other ability (GM approval required) in step 4.
                  4. In step 4, choose Custom species advantage… and enter the advantage and its companion complication.

                  Example

                  Rhessk (tier 1). Small, quick, burrow-dwelling traders from a moon of the Tessan core worlds, long-time clients of the dynasties. Adjustments: Agility +1, Presence +1, Body −2. Core rule: night-adapted: see in near-darkness, −1 in bright light. Species advantage: Tunnel-Runner: +2 to Athletics in tight spaces. Companion: Client People: your family’s dynasty calls on you; accept the errand.

                  Threats, weapons and Edges for your table

                  A GM can add their own threats, weapons and Edges. Keep them in line with the book’s:

                  • Threats. A minor foe has 1 box; an ordinary one 3; a tough one 4 or 5; a rare horror 6. Attack targets run 11 to 13 for most, 14 or 15 for the dangerous. Dodge runs 7 to 10. Give it one special trait, said plainly, and decide what it does before play: toughness, a weakness or armor works as in Armor, toughness and weaknesses. For a tougher version of any threat, add +1 to its targets and one box; for a weaker one, subtract.
                  • Weapons. Hits mark 1 box for fists, knives and arrows; 2 for swords and guns; 3 for the heavy and the point-blank; 4 only for explosives and the monstrous. Give a weapon a reach (melee) or a range band, and its shots if they run out.
                  • Edges. An Edge is worth about as much as one of the book’s: a narrow, useful benefit, often once per session or per job. Say exactly what it does.
                  • Cards. One subject, what’s true about it and what that permits: as narrow as a card earned in play.
                  • Powers. Write what it does at each Class, I to VI, stepping up as the setting’s own powers do; anything that bends minds, time or death needs the GM’s approval.
                  • Spells. A new hex, cantrip or psionic power matches the setting’s own: an attack marks 1 or 2 boxes at Close or Short range, and anything stronger says who resists and what it costs.
                  • Rituals. Give a ritual its weight (Minor 2 segments, Significant 4, Major 6), the time a roll takes, what it does and its price.

                  In the creator. The GM view’s Homebrew tab keeps your threats, weapons, Edges, origins, advantages, cards, powers, spells and rituals. They then work like the book’s, marked homebrew: threats in the Encounter panel and on the battle map, weapons in characters’ gear and the roller, Edges, origins, advantages, powers and spells among the creator’s choices (a homebrew origin follows the steps above, with the tier, attribute changes, origin skills and origin advantages you set), cards where findings are recorded, and rituals in a ritual book beside Rituals by heart. Players get them when they join your shared table, or from a homebrew file you give them. Bonuses chosen from the tab’s menus are worked out for you: a weapon’s accuracy, strong hits and what it’s made of; a threat’s hard hide, weaknesses, what alone can hurt it and how hard it is to hit; an Edge’s skill, Dodge or Move bonus and extra defense; an attack spell cast in the Encounter panel. Anything else is a note the GM applies at the table.

                  Your campaign

                  The GM view’s Campaign tab holds the campaign itself: its premise, an outline of adventures, its people, places and factions, and its sessions (the plan before, the log after). Roll fills any of them from the setting’s own tables, its adventure seeds, key characters, places, threats and names, and you change what you like before you keep it. Everything stays yours until you share it; then the players see its public part on their play tab, never a secret or your notes.

                  Triggers: cards that open the story. A step of the outline can have a trigger: it stays locked until the group holds the cards it names (a subject, or several) and as many cards as you ask for. The moment a character’s cards meet it, the step unlocks for good and the GM view tells you what happens. Share a locked step to give the players a goal (“it opens with a card about the drowned god”), or keep it to yourself. Cards are earned through discovery, so a trigger makes finding things out the way the story moves: the next chapter waits for the group to learn what it needs.

                  Complications

                  Choose one complication. These are sources of meaningful choices, not constant penalties. The GM proposes a concrete problem and offers one Resolve point if you accept it. Every complication needs a trigger agreed with the GM; the creator suggests three for each.

                  Complication What it does
                  Debt-Bound You owe a dynasty, a bank or a syndicate. Accept the collector’s demand.
                  Unregistered You’re a psionic who has never been tested, or has a forged result. Accept the danger at every screening and checkpoint.
                  Wanted A government, house or corporation wants you. Accept the hunters.
                  Hegemony Bounty An imperial house has put a price on you. Accept the bounty hunter.
                  Implant Upkeep Your implants need parts, power and care. Accept the cost or the malfunction.
                  Idealist You won’t compromise your principles. Accept the cost of keeping them.
                  Greedy You can’t walk away from profit. Accept the risk to grab it.
                  Old Rival Someone is always a step ahead or behind you. Accept their interference.
                  Corporate Leash Your employer owns your contract. Accept the order you don’t like.
                  Honor-Bound You keep your word, your oaths and your people’s customs. Accept the setback.
                  Survivor’s Guilt You lived when others didn’t. Accept the reckless choice to make it right.
                  Can’t Leave a Mystery Alone A strange signal or ruin pulls you in. Accept the detour or the danger.
                  Protects Others You shield the weak at your own risk. Accept the cost.
                  Stim Habit You lean on combat stims or calm-patches. Accept the craving or the crash.
                  Exile You can’t go home. Accept the scorn or the hunters of your own people.
                  Dangerous Knowledge You know a corridor, a crime or a name someone would kill to bury. Accept the danger.
                  Reckless You jump first and think later. Accept the danger.
                  Distrusts AI You won’t trust a machine mind. Accept the cost of refusing its help.
                  Culture Shock You misread other peoples’ customs. Accept the misunderstanding.

                  Quick reference

                  Fine weapon or tool: +2 to one narrow, agreed use of a skill; never with an advantage on the same roll; never to Dodge, Parry or Block.

                  Creation: attributes start at 10, adjusted by species (always totaling zero), plus 5 points; maximum 13 plus any species bonus. 3 points split between species tier and Edges. Specialist: one Specialty and nine Trained. Expert: one Expert at +5 and seven Trained. One advantage (general or species) and one complication; an optional Allegiance.

                  Skills: Untrained = attribute −4; Trained = attribute +1; Specialty = attribute +3; Expert (Expert) = attribute +5.

                  Modifiers: favorable +2; ordinary 0; difficult −2; very difficult −4; extreme −6. Natural 3–4 succeeds; natural 17–18 fails.

                  Assistance: success +1; success by 5 or more +2; 18 causes a complication. One assistant per roll.

                  Near misses: fail by 1–2 and the GM may offer success at a cost; never on a natural 17–18.

                  Clocks: 2, 4, 6 or 8 segments. Danger clocks fill on failures and time; progress clocks fill on successes (2 segments on success by 5).

                  Move: 5 yd, +1 per 2 points of Agility + Body above 20, +1 Trained Athletics or +2 Specialty/Expert, ± species speed; run (no action) twice that. Threats 8 yd. Wounded −2 yd; seriously wounded half, no run. Hard going: half. Stepping away is free. Reach: 1 yd fists, knives, clubs; 2 yd swords, axes; 3 yd spears, polearms.

                  Combat: move plus one action. Hit → one defense a round (Dodge, Parry or Block; −1 to −3 against a clean hit; Additional Defense: a second, at −2) → weapon effect. Dodge = Agility −2 plus Athletics training (+0, +1, +2). Parry −3, Block −2 plus the shield. Aim: +1. Telling hit (by 5+ or natural 3–4): the attacker picks an effect the weapon can deliver (pin: weapon in hand or grapple only), which never adds boxes or kills outright; called shot −2 (small target −4). A 2-box weapon that brings you to three boxes leaves you Dying; at three boxes, another 2-box hit kills.

                  Medicine: stabilize in one action. Field care clears 1 box (2 on margin 5+). Proper care gives +2 and clears 2 (3 on margin 5+). Each set of injuries (one fight or incident) gets one field and one proper-care attempt; more need better care, a new treatment or recovery time. Rest clears a box in a day at 1 box, three days at 2, a week at 3 (in someone’s care).

                  Resolve: start each session with two. Reroll, reduce an injury by one box, shrug off a telling hit, or establish a small preparation. Earn one from an accepted complication.

                  This book is for whoever runs the game. It opens with a first adventure, ready to run, and gathers what the GM reaches for at the table: job seeds, the threats and enemy ships with their numbers, and how to use the GM view’s battle map and Encounter panel. The rules themselves are in the Players’ Guide; this book builds on them.

                  Your first job

                  A ready-to-run salvage job to start a campaign with. Everything it needs is here, and the pregenerated characters in the creator are written into it.

                  The first job: Salvage Rights

                  A starter job for three to seven crew, for one or two sessions. A salvage run down a corridor that isn’t on any map, to a colony ship lost for 140 years, against a corporation, a closing corridor and the question of who a ship belongs to. It shows off the corridors, the crew’s ship and its tracks, a ship fight, a data record and a Countdown. It’s written for the seven pregenerated characters, and works with any.

                  The hook. The crew’s next Debt payment is due, and a Tessan debt-broker, Ves Oro-Lan, has an offer: salvage the data core of the colony ship Long Patience, which vanished in a corridor collapse 140 years ago, and the broker clears a box of Debt and pays 2,000 credits besides. A probe found the ship’s beacon last week, at the far end of a corridor that collapsed with it. The guild charts say that corridor is gone. Ilvi Saradh’s AI, Quill, remembers it, and says it’s open again. Give each crew member a reason of their own:

                  • Thessk Varo-Hun: the salvage claim belongs to her dynasty’s old creditors. Get there first, and the claim is the crew’s.
                  • Kesh of the Seventh Hive: an open corridor to the old colony worlds is worth more to her hive than the ship.
                  • Rook: the implant payments are overdue, and this is the only offer on the board.
                  • Ilvi Saradh: Quill was right, and the guild must not find out how they knew.
                  • Dr. Anwe Tal: the Long Patience carried a seed vault from the world she’s rebuilding, before the strip-mining.
                  • Brakka: the ship’s last port of call was a Hegemony world. Whatever is aboard, the Hegemony will want it.
                  • Sable: a 140-year-old encrypted core. Nobody else alive can open it.

                  What’s really happening. The Long Patience isn’t dead. Its 312 colonists are asleep in cryo, and its AI, the Warden, has kept them alive for 140 years, growing the hull around them like a shell. The corridor has reopened for a few days only; it’s drifting closed again. Ves Oro-Lan sold the same coordinates to Vantor Reclamation, a salvage corporation, which has sent a team to strip the core and leave the rest. And under the Human–Tessan Accord, a ship with living crew aboard is not salvage: wake the colonists and the claim is void.

                  1. The offer. Ves meets the crew in a dockside tea house, smiling. A Psychology roll notices the broker keeps checking the departures board. Pressed, Ves admits “another party has expressed interest”. The crew can push for better terms: Commerce, and success clears the Debt box up front.

                  2. The run. The corridor is a Navigation roll for Ilvi, with Quill’s help (+2): a success gets them through clean; a failure takes them through anyway, but the ship’s transit is logged at the junction, and Heat marks a box. On the far side: a drift of old wreckage, and the Long Patience, twelve kilometers of hull grown over with something like bark.

                  3. Company. A Vantor Reclamation corporate frigate is already there, and it hails them: back off, or be fired on. This is a chance to run a ship fight (Ships in a fight, in the Players’ Guide), or to talk, bluff or sneak past. Sensors can find the frigate’s blind spot; Sable can spoof its registry; a good hail buys an exchange. If the fight goes badly, the frigate lets them limp to the derelict: Vantor wants the core, not a second wreck.

                  4. Boarding. Inside, the hull is warm and breathing. Start a data record for the Long Patience (Data records, in the Players’ Guide); this is the setting’s own example, A living hull. The clues, and who finds them best:

                  • The cryo decks (Medicine, Science): 312 colonists alive, vital signs low and steady. Somebody has been changing the fluids.
                  • The grown hull (Science, Engineering): the bark-stuff is a lattice of engineered cells, fed by the reactor and shaped by the ship’s own systems.
                  • The bridge log (Computers, Investigation): the last human entry is 140 years old; the next hundred thousand entries are the Warden’s, one a day, all the same: Still waiting.
                  • The seed vault (Science, or Dr. Anwe Tal’s own knowledge): intact. The world she’s rebuilding could be green in a generation.

                  When the crew cuts into anything vital, or the first investigation roll fails, start a Countdown of 6: the corridor is drifting closed. Every scene ticks it; when it fills, the corridor shuts for another hundred years, with whoever is still on this side.

                  5. The Warden. The Warden speaks through the ship: a slow, polite voice that has had no one to talk to for 140 years. It wants the colonists taken home. It knows the corridor is closing, and it can’t fly the ship alone: the drive needs a navigator and an engineer. Sable and Ilvi can talk to it as an equal; Rook and Brakka recognize a soldier still at their post.

                  6. Vantor boards. A Vantor team cuts in to take the core: a Syndicate enforcer (hired muscle), two Combat drones and a Corporate assassin who would rather not be seen. They have orders to vent the cryo decks to make the salvage legal. This is the big fight, in the ship’s grown corridors.

                  7. The choice. With the Countdown running out, the crew chooses: take the core and the money, and leave the colonists to sleep another century; wake them, and the claim is void; or fly the Long Patience home, with the Warden at the helm and the crew’s ship alongside. Flying it home means a Piloting or Navigation roll against the closing corridor, and nobody pays them for it.

                  Rewards. Ves’s 2,000 credits and a box of Debt, if they bring the core. A data record on the living hull, and a friend in the Warden if the colonists live. If they bring 312 people home, Reputation marks a box, for the good: the ports talk about it for years. If Vantor learns who stopped them, Heat marks one.

                  Threats. Corporate frigate (Enemy ships); Syndicate enforcer; Combat drone ×2; Corporate assassin. The Warden is a Rogue AI that never attacks: it must be talked down, isolated or erased, and erasing it kills the colonists.

                  Running jobs and missions

                  Job seeds

                  Roll 3d6 on each table and read the total, or pick what you like. Middle results come up most often; the strangest sit at 3, 4, 17 and 18. The GM view in the creator rolls these for you and can start the clock.

                  3d6 Job or mission Place The trouble

                  4 Broker a peace inside the Hegemony The Hegemony’s throne world An imperial fleet stranded for 300 years emerges
                  5 Deliver cargo through a contested corridor A Tessan exchange station A corridor is collapsing
                  6 Collect, or escape, a debt A Concord colony on the frontier A Hegemony fleet emerges from a reopened corridor
                  7 Find a missing ship A Vael flotilla Mandate inquisitors are screening everyone
                  8 Escort a refugee convoy A Brulvek shipyard rusting in orbit A rogue AI has taken over the systems
                  9 Recover a stolen archive A Veyari library world A Kel radical cell plans an attack
                  10 Smuggle a psionic past the Mandates A Khaum cavern city A plague engineered with biotech

                  Threats

                  Opponents use the same rules as the characters. Minor opponents have one box: any hit that gets through takes them out of the fight.

                  Threat Attack (target) Dodge Boxes Weapon Trait
                  Station security or thug (minor) Firearms 11 7 1 Stunner or pistol Numbers. Three or four of them; they back off when half are down.
                  Combat drone (minor, swarms) Firearms 12 9 1 each Light laser (2) Swarm. Kill its controller or jam its link, and the swarm drops.
                  Pirate raider Firearms 12, Close Combat 12 9 2 Slug carbine Boarders. Hit fast, grab what they can, run.
                  Tessan debt collector Commerce 15, Firearms 12 8 3 Bonded-agent contract Lien. Can lawfully seize your ship or gear; in Tessan space, resisting marks Debt and Heat.
                  Syndicate enforcer (Augment) Close Combat 15, Firearms 13 10 4 Implant blades (2), shotgun Chromed. Hits marking 2 or more boxes mark one fewer.

                  Adjusting difficulty. For a tougher version, add +1 to its targets and one box; for a weaker one, subtract.

                  Enemy ships

                  Ship Pilot / Gunner Hull Weapons Trait
                  Pirate raider 12 / 12 3 Laser battery, missiles (2) Boarders. Wants your cargo, not your ship; tries to close to Close.
                  Customs cutter 13 / 12 4 Laser battery Papers. Demands an inspection first; resisting marks Heat.
                  Corporate frigate 13 / 14 5 Lasers, missiles (4) Armor. Ignores one 1-box hit each exchange.
                  Syndicate gunrunner 14 / 13 4 Lasers, point defense Fast. +2 to the range contest.

                  Data records

                  Running investigations and recording what the crew learns. The rules players use are in the Data records chapter of the Players’ Guide; here is the GM view’s Discovery panel, for clocks and records.

                  Making data records

                  For the GM: when a data record is earned, and how to write one. A data record is a record of what the characters established, so writing it well matters more than how often you hand one out.

                  1. Decide that something is established. A data record is earned when a discovery clock fills, or when the characters see or test something themselves, hear it from a source you judge reliable, or are told it by the subject itself with evidence to back it up. A guess, however right, isn’t established, and neither is a rumor. Ask what supports their idea; when the answer is good, let them act on it, and give the data record once they’ve confirmed it.
                  2. Write the finding narrowly. One fact, in the words the characters would use, and no more than they found out: “bright light drove it back”, not “it fears light”. Two separate facts make two data records. Never write the subject’s whole truth onto a data record; later discoveries add more data records.
                  3. Write its limits. What the finding doesn’t show: how often it was seen, under what conditions, and what is still unknown. The limits are what keep the next investigation interesting.
                  4. Note the evidence or source. What they saw, tested, read or were told, and by whom. A source’s reputation doesn’t make it right: if it was only probably true, the limits say so.
                  5. Charge the price. A data record from a discovery clock costs nothing more: the scenes, failed rolls and pushes were its price. Any other source has its price (see Earning a data record): choose the one that fits how they learned it, and mark it.
                  6. Choose the owner and the recipients. Whoever did the finding owns the data record. Everyone who was there, or heard it from a reliable source, gets a shared copy.
                  7. Record it. In the GM view’s Discovery panel: Mint a full clock’s data record, or use Record a finding without a clock, which marks the price for you. Then save everyone’s characters to file, so the players’ sheets carry it. A player can also write a data record on their own sheet, when you agree it’s been earned.

                  Example: The Kessel Deep derelict. Established: Its reactor powers down whenever the corridor beacon goes silent. Limits: Seen twice, from outside the hull; not what restarts it. Source: The crew’s own sensor logs (scanned or tested firsthand). Cost: Countdown +1 (the hours spent watching it).

                  • When a later finding disagrees. Write a new data record that says what they now know; the old one stays on the sheet as what they believed then, and the new one’s limits can say so.
                  • A data record is never proof of identity. Holding a data record about one subject doesn’t prove that the thing in front of them is that subject: the Identify phase does.
                  • Weaknesses work anyway. Don’t hold back a real weakness because no one holds the data record: if they try it, it works.
                  • Classified Archive. Agree each starting data record with its player before play: it must come from the character’s role or species, be narrow, and be a real secret: something that isn’t in any database or published record. Make sure it fits what you know to be true, adjust it if it doesn’t, and keep a note of it.

                  Example data records

                  Seven subjects the crew might investigate, each with what goes wrong on a failed roll or a success at a cost in each phase, what its record permits, and the skill that lets a character skip Confront. A failure is where the GM may start a Countdown, when the stakes are real.

                  Halvane lattice core

                  A crystalline power system found on derelict Halvane haulers, the work of a people lost behind a collapsed corridor. Ordinary engineering can’t read it.

                  • Confront the unknown: get the core to respond. On a failure: it pulses and drains nearby power cells; suits and tools lose charge.
                  • Identify: learn it feeds on the crew’s own power signatures. On a failure: resonance builds; the GM may start a Countdown to critical.
                  • Uncover: find the harmonic frequency that controls it. On a failure: a feedback surge injures whoever is linked to it.
                  • Permits: waking, powering down or rerouting any Halvane lattice core. Skill: Engineering.

                  The Warden of the Ashkarr

                  One damaged military intelligence, the Warden, still running aboard the derelict Hegemony warship Ashkarr. An AI Minder’s training covers AIs in general; this record covers only the Warden’s own command authority.

                  • Confront the unknown: get it to acknowledge the crew. On a failure: it activates the ship’s defenses; the GM may start a Countdown to full lockdown.
                  • Identify: learn it is still executing a wartime directive and takes the crew for enemy boarders. On a failure: it vents a section or seals bulkheads, splitting the party.
                  • Uncover: find its original command authority code (the captain’s quarters, the black-box logs, a dead officer’s implant). On a failure: it detects the tampering and purges the trail; another source must be found.
                  • Permits: issuing orders the Warden obeys, or shutting it down cleanly without tripping its failsafes. Skill: Computers.

                  A corridor engine

                  An ancient machine, inert until approached. Corridors are natural folds, and no one builds them; but where a fold already runs close, this machine forces open a mouth that no chart shows. Who made it, and why, is a question for another investigation.

                  • Confront the unknown: detect that it’s active, not wreckage. On a failure: a spatial pulse throws crew or objects a short distance.
                  • Identify: learn it is still keyed to a far mouth, and something on the other side is listening. On a failure: the mouth half-opens; something comes through, or a signal goes out.
                  • Uncover: decode its address glyphs and its sealing sequence. On a failure: it locks onto a random mouth; the GM may start a Countdown to an unstable opening.
                  • Permits: opening its mouth to a known destination along the fold, or sealing it for good. Skill: Science.

                  Spatial fracture

                  An unstable region where space folds on itself; the sensors return contradictory readings.

                  • Confront the unknown: map the fracture’s edge. On a failure: the ship clips it; mark Hull, or a system goes offline.
                  • Identify: learn it shifts in a cycle tied to an outside rhythm (a pulsar, a nearby drive’s signature). On a failure: time slips; the crew loses hours.
                  • Uncover: plot the safe corridor that opens on each cycle. On a failure: the ship is caught mid-fold; the GM starts a Countdown to hull failure.
                  • Permits: navigating this fracture, and fractures of its kind, safely. Skill: Navigation.

                  A living hull

                  A living ship that treats intruders as an infection.

                  • Confront the unknown: realize the ship is alive and aware. On a failure: tissue walls close passages or secrete irritants.
                  • Identify: learn its immune response escalates with each disturbance, and in the end digests foreign matter. On a failure: antibody organisms attack; the GM may start a Countdown to its full immune response.
                  • Uncover: find the chemical or bio-signature it accepts as self (from its dead crew, its nursery, its pilot cradle). On a failure: the wrong signature marks the crew as its first target.
                  • Permits: moving through the ship unopposed, and coaxing its doors, systems or will to cooperate. Skill: Science or Medicine.

                  Corporate black-site encryption

                  A proprietary security layer guarding a corporate facility or data vault.

                  • Confront the unknown: recognize it as an adaptive, corporation-specific system, not standard encryption. On a failure: the attempt is logged; mark Heat.
                  • Identify: learn it has a dead-man response: tampering calls corporate security or wipes the vault. On a failure: the GM may start a Countdown to the security response or the wipe.
                  • Uncover: obtain a valid credential pattern (a defector, a stolen badge, a maintenance back door). On a failure: the credential is flagged, and its source is burned.
                  • Permits: bypassing this corporation’s black-site security, or forging credentials it accepts. Skill: Computers.

                  An alien weapon cache

                  A stockpile of weapons built by a hostile species, perhaps still being used against the crew.

                  • Confront the unknown: survive or witness the weapons in use. On a failure: one discharges, or is turned on the crew.
                  • Identify: learn they’re keyed to their makers’ biology, or tuned to a frequency. On a failure: a weapon self-destructs or alerts its owners.
                  • Uncover: find how they fail (a frequency that overloads them, a biometric spoof). On a failure: a booby trap goes off; if the cache is rigged to blow, the GM may start a Countdown.
                  • Permits: disabling these weapons in a fight (a telling hit’s break-gear effect works on them even in the makers’ hands), or turning them against their makers. Skill: Engineering or Firearms.

                  Rival clocks

                  A careful crew can investigate without ever starting a Countdown. To keep the pressure on, give the discovery a rival (see Discovery clocks). The corridors are full of them:

                  Rival What they want
                  A Draelin cartographic guild Corridor data, which they sell to both sides
                  The Veyari archives The discovery preserved, perhaps out of the crew’s reach
                  A corporation Salvage and technology it can own and sell
                  A Hegemony house Imperial ruins and technology returned
                  A syndicate Anything it can fence

                  The Discovery panel

                  The GM view’s Discovery panel runs discovery clocks and the Countdown they race (it stays idle until you Start the Countdown after a failed roll or a success at a cost). Start a clock with its segments per phase (or a plain progress clock for a repair or a task in the same race), and fill it as the investigation rolls succeed. It stops at the Identify gate until you name the subject; then it shows every data record the characters in the GM view already hold for it. The Failed roll and Push buttons tick the track for how they were digging. When a clock fills, Mint gives the primary investigator the data record and everyone you tick as present a shared copy. Record a finding without a clock gives a data record for something established directly (seen or tested, a reliable account, a creature’s word with evidence behind it) to whoever you tick, and marks its price: the track or the Countdown that source costs. Save all to file afterwards, so the players’ character files carry it. The Discord bot’s /discovery and /cards commands do the same at a table that plays online.

                  The GM’s tools

                  The battle map

                  The GM view of the character creator has a battle map for fights where it helps to see who is where. It is a tool, not a rule: everything on it follows the Personal combat rules in the Players’ Guide, and a fight without it works the same way. Open How to use the map on the map itself for the buttons, step by step.

                  Two kinds of map.

                  • A hex map for fights where position matters: cover, doorways, who can reach whom. The GM chooses what one hex is: 1 yard for a brawl in a room, 5 or 10 yards for a street, 50 for open ground. Dragging a token or measuring shows the distance and its range band, so the GM can read the penalty from the Range table in the Players’ Guide. A token can have a height (a flier, a sniper on a roof), and the distance counts it.
                  • A range track for fights where only distance matters: a chase, a running fight across open country. It has a lane for the crew and one for each range band. Moving a token into the next lane moves it one band in or out.

                  Tokens. The GM places the crew with one button. Their tokens stay linked to the characters in the GM view: marking Injury, Dying, the stunned condition or a Resolve point on a token marks it on the character, and the other way round. Opponents come from the setting’s threats with their boxes filled in. Their pips fill as they are hurt, and a token whose boxes are all marked is taken out.

                  Keeping a map. The map stays in the GM’s browser. Save map to file keeps both maps, their pictures and tokens in one file, to prepare a fight ahead of time or share it with another GM.

                  Ship fight. In this setting the range track is for ship fights, with the bands Close (under 10 km), Short (up to 1,000 km), Medium (up to 10,000 km), Long (up to 100,000 km), Extreme (about a light-second). Add our ship places a token linked to the crew’s Hull track, so damage marked on the map is marked on the sheet. Enemy ships come from the Enemy ships table with their Hull boxes. Each lane is a range band from our ship. When the pilots make their opposed Piloting roll, drag the enemy one lane in or out. Weapons take −2 one band beyond their range and −4 two bands beyond.

                  The Encounter panel

                  The GM view also has an Encounter panel that runs a fight by the Personal combat rules and shows every roll. Add characters from the GM view and opponents from the Threats table (or make one up on the spot), then start: it keeps the turn order by Agility, and for each attack works out the range, the defense (Dodge, Parry or Block, one a round, and a second at −2 with Additional Defense), the boxes marked and any telling hit, offering a Resolve point choices at the moment they apply. Hits land on the character cards and the battle map, and with gritty combat on, grievous wounds are rolled and kept. The panel keeps a log and a summary of the fight, which can be saved to a file. It’s a helper, not a rule: the GM can rule any result differently, and the log says so.

                  The shared table. The GM can start a shared table from the GM view and give the players its code; each player joins from their character’s Play tab. While they’re connected, every roll from a sheet is rolled by the table server, so the whole table sees the same dice as they land, in a live log on the Play tab and on the GM view, along with who rolled, against what, and any telling hit. A point reroll answers its own roll, once. Each player’s character is shared with the GM too: it appears among the GM view’s characters, marked at the table, and its injuries, points, ammunition and form stay in step both ways, whether they’re changed on the sheet, on the GM’s card or in an encounter. In a fight, each player’s Play tab shows the GM’s battle map and the encounter’s turn order and latest results; a player drags their own token, and on their turn sends the GM what they’ll do, which the GM puts into the Encounter panel and runs. The GM can remove a player from the table, and give the table a new code: everyone at it moves with it, and the old code stops working. Without a table, the roller works exactly as it always has.

                  The crew’s ship and the job board

                  The GM view has three tools for the corridors, in Clocks and tools:

                  • The crew’s ship. Its name, type and quirk, picked or rolled. Players see it on their play tab, above the crew’s tracks, through the shared table. When its trouble bites, someone earns Resolve.
                  • The job board. Roll an offer gives a patron, the job, the pay and the catch; re-roll any part. Roll two or three for a port, and keep the catch to yourself until a Commerce roll or the job reveals it.
                  • A derelict. What it was, what happened, what’s still aboard, the danger and the prize. Start its data record, and a Countdown if the danger is a clock.

                      Clocks

                      Danger clocks fill on failures and time; progress clocks fill on successes. Tap a segment to fill up to it.

                      Debt, Heat, Reputation and Hull

                      Shared by the whole crew. Borrowing, breaking the law, psionic slips and fame can mark a box; paying up, lying low and quiet work can clear one between jobs.

                      Quick reference

                      Resolution
                      3d6 at or below adjusted skill. Natural 3–4 always succeeds; 17–18 always fails. Margin = target − roll.
                      Opposed
                      Success beats failure; both succeed → larger margin wins; ties and double failures favor the defender.
                      Combat
                      Move up to your Move and take one action. Hit → target may defend once per round: Dodge, Parry or Block → weapon effect. Partial cover −2.
                      Defending
                      One defense a round; Additional Defense: a second, at −2, never twice against one attack. Dodge: Agility −2 + Athletics. Parry a weapon in hand or fists: Close Combat or Close Combat −3. Block a weapon in hand, fists or a missile with a shield or anything that stands in for one: Close Combat −2 + the shield's bonus (never a gunshot or blast); an improvised one breaks on a 2+ box hit. Attack succeeded by 3–4: defense −1; 5–6: −2; 7+: −3. Aim (one action): +1 to your next attack on that target.
                      Telling hit
                      Hit by 5+ or a natural 3–4, not defended: the attacker picks one effect the weapon can deliver (disarm; knock down, in hand or a 2+ box shot: standing uses their move; pin, in hand or a grapple only: their next action frees them; rattle −2; break gear, not bare-handed: out of use until an action fixes it; open them up +2; precise). Called shot: −2 (small target −4), and any hit gets the effect. No extra boxes, never an outright kill. Shrug it off: Hard to put down (once a fight) or a point.
                      Range
                      Close 10 yd, Short 25 yd, Medium 100 yd, Long 300 yd, Extreme 1,000 yd. Within a weapon's effective band: no penalty; one band beyond −2, two −4, farther out of range.
                      Move
                      5 yd, +1 per 2 points of Agility + Body above 20, +1 Trained Athletics or +2 Specialty/Expert, ± species speed. Run (no action): twice that. Threats: 8 yd. Wounded −2 yd; seriously wounded half, no running. Hard going (climbing, swimming, snow, rubble): half. Stepping away from a fight is free.
                      Reach
                      1 yd: fists, knives, clubs, claws. 2 yd: swords, axes, maces. 3 yd: spears, polearms.
                      Dying
                      A 2-box weapon that brings you to 3 boxes: Dying; dead at the end of the scene unless stabilized (one action, Medicine, medkit). At 3 boxes, another 2-box hit kills.
                      Medicine
                      Stabilize: one action. Field care clears 1 box (2 on margin 5+). Proper care gives +2, clears 2 (3 on margin 5+). One field and one proper-care attempt per set of injuries (one fight or incident); more need better care, a new treatment or recovery time.
                      Rest
                      Clearing one box: a full day at 1 box, at least three days at 2, a week at 3 (and only once someone has stabilized or treated you).
                      Resolve
                      Reroll (keep second), reduce an injury by one box, shrug off a telling hit, or establish a small preparation.
                      Damage
                      Fists, batons: 1 box. Pistols, lasers, carbines, blades, claws: 2. Plasma rifle, coilgun: 3 and Dying. Stunner: Body −2 roll, no box.
                      Firearms
                      Slug pistol 12, laser pistol 20, carbine 30, plasma rifle 10. Burst: 3 shots, +1 (carbine). Covering fire: 3. Reload: one action. Natural 18 jams.
                      Psionics
                      Powers: an action and a Psionics roll; known: Trained 2, Specialty 3, Expert 4. Failure or natural 18 marks Heat. Mandate scanners detect active powers.
                      Corridors
                      Transit: Navigation (old charts −2, years old or unstable −4). Each step deeper halves the time, −2. Fail by 3+ deep: Body roll or 1 box. Natural 18: misjump.
                      Metric drive
                      Up to 3× light speed (civilian 1–2×). In-system: hours. Between stars: light-years ÷ 3 in years. Not in corridors, near mouths or deep in gravity wells.
                      Ship combat
                      Space bands: Close <10 km, Short 1,000 km, Medium 10,000 km, Long 100,000 km, Extreme a light-second. Opposed Piloting each exchange shifts range one band. Point defense Close 1, lasers Medium 1, missiles Long 2, coilgun Extreme 3 Hull boxes.
                      Captain
                      One order an exchange: Command (Leadership, +2 to a station), Read the enemy (Psychology), Hail (Diplomacy or Deception vs Will), Rally (Leadership).
                      Tracks
                      Debt (what you owe), Heat (who's after you), Reputation (who knows you), Hull (your ship). 4 boxes each; clear by paying up, lying low, quiet work or a dock between jobs.
